# karpo-apple-silicon

> Unofficial community port that runs MachinePulse's Karpo Decision models (karpo-decision-31B and karpo-decision-12B, the Gemma 4 family checkpoints) on Apple Silicon Macs. One small PyTorch patch for the MPS (Metal) GPU, plus an experimental MLX path with 8-bit and 4-bit quantized weights. Apache-2.0. Not affiliated with MachinePulse or Google.

## The short answer

Karpo Decision as published needs an NVIDIA GPU. On a Mac the checkpoint loads, then the first `decide()` call fails with `NotImplementedError: The operator 'aten::_flash_attention_forward' is not currently implemented for the MPS device`, because the sliding-window layers call `torch.nn.attention.varlen.varlen_attn`, which PyTorch only provides for CUDA. Calling `karpo_apple_silicon.install()` before the first `decide()` replaces that call with banded masked attention. Without CUDA it also replaces the global layers' attention call with one that computes the same result 256 query rows at a time, which keeps long requests correct and lets the model run on a CPU. On CPU the real 12B has been run on an Apple Silicon Mac with version 0.2.0 and gave the Apple GPU's answers. `PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1` does not fix the original error.

## Install and use

```bash
pip install "karpo-decision @ git+https://github.com/machinepulse-ai/karpo-decision@c52d3507a254d3ad8423726c6bc6568c99113e7d"
pip install "karpo-apple-silicon @ git+https://github.com/fluxcodestudio/karpo-apple-silicon@v0.2.0"
```

```python
import karpo_apple_silicon
karpo_apple_silicon.install()
from karpo_decision.decider import Decider
decider = Decider.from_pretrained("path/to/karpo-decision-31B", device="mps")
```

## Facts

- Hardware: Apple Silicon Macs (M1, M2, M3, M4 and later), macOS 14 or later. Memory: about 96 GB for the 31B as shipped (62.6 GB of weights), more than 24.0 GB for the 12B. On a 96 GB MacBook Pro (M2 Max) with most other apps closed, version 0.2.0 loaded the 31B and answered requests as shipped and converted to float16; in single runs a 1,049-token request took 11.1 s in bfloat16 and 6.6 s in float16, a 7,464-token one 83 s and 51 s, and a 10,196-token one 128 s and 107 s, with swap steady between 9.6 and 11.5 GB. Beyond about 10,000 tokens the 31B as shipped swaps on 96 GB and slows sharply (21 minutes at 23,627 tokens, 36 at 31,489, both answered correctly); the 12B answers a 31,489-token request in 177 s (124 s in float16) and the 8-bit MLX copy of the 31B in 399 s.
- Less memory: the MLX path runs the 31B from quantized copies, downloads of 34.0 GB at 8 bits and 19.3 GB at 4 bits (31.6 and 18.0 GB in memory, in the units macOS reports), text requests only.
- Ready-made MLX weights: https://huggingface.co/jonnyArt/karpo-decision-31B-mlx-8bit and https://huggingface.co/jonnyArt/karpo-decision-31B-mlx-4bit
- Accuracy against MachinePulse's published 31B results (340 requests, 1,606 questions), measured twice: with version 0.1.0 on a Mac Studio (M2 Ultra) and with version 0.2.0 on a MacBook Pro (M2 Max). PyTorch on MPS, bfloat16 as shipped, changed 1 top answer in each run (mean difference 0.0011 with 0.1.0, 0.0012 with 0.2.0; largest 0.103 and 0.090); MLX 8-bit changed 2 in each run (0.0016 and 0.0014); MLX 4-bit, run on 145 of those requests, changed 3 of 681 in each run (0.0067 both times). With both versions' attention on the same loaded 31B, requests shorter than the 1,024-token window gave the same answers to within 0.00005; on the longer requests examined the versions differed by up to 0.037 in bfloat16 and 0.007 in float16. The reworked MLX loader and forward pass (version 0.2.0) have been checked on small random models, and both published folders have the required tensor names and shapes. On the real 4-bit weights version 0.2.0 gave the same top answer as version 0.1.0 on 71 questions (largest probability difference 0.061) with lower peak memory on long requests (23.3 GB to 20.9 GB at 7,464 tokens) and no measurable change in time; on the real 8-bit weights it likewise gave the same top answers on those 71 questions (largest difference 0.040), peaking at 35.6 GB instead of 40.4 GB at 10,196 tokens. On the real 31B in bfloat16, version 0.2.0 gave the same top answers as version 0.1.0 on 31 questions of invented requests (28 of them near-certain; largest probability difference 0.037), and the same top answers as the MLX copies on 71 questions (66 near-certain; largest difference 0.052 for the 8-bit copy and 0.159 for the 4-bit one); converted to float16 it gave the same 71 top answers as in bfloat16 (largest difference 0.028).
- Long requests: without CUDA karpo-decision's global layers compute their attention over a whole request in one call, and version 0.1.0 of this port left that as it was. On a 96 GB Mac the real 12B answered a 23,627-token request with noise that way, with no error. Version 0.2.0 makes the same call 256 query rows at a time; with it the 12B, the 31B and both MLX copies answered requests of up to 31,489 tokens (karpo-decision's default limit is 32,768 per sequence) with every checkable answer right.
- Not covered or not checked: the Qwen-family Karpo models (0.8B to 9B and 27B-act), images, comparison with the published results beyond 8,072 tokens or for the 12B (no per-request results are published for it), GGUF / llama.cpp / Ollama. AMD and Intel GPUs have not been checked.
- Port version 0.2.0; tested with karpo-decision 0.1.0 (commits 6600011eb5cf and c52d3507a254, which have the same source files), torch 2.15.0, transformers 5.23.0, mlx 0.32.4, mlx-lm 0.32.2. The installer compares pip's recorded upstream commit because the upstream version has not changed between commits, and checks the signatures of both functions it replaces before it swaps either.
